13.3.4 Equality Movement further observed in its statement to the CGRS:

‘The situation has drastically deteriorated after the adoption of the “Law on Family Values and Minors” that introduced additional barriers to educational inclusiveness and obstructed efforts to combat widespread homophobic discourses in society… In direct contradiction to the principle of inclusiveness, the law prohibits the incorporation of SOGIESC related information into all types of formal educational programs, as well as the dissemination and/or facilitating the dissemination of such information within formal educational institutions, including schools, universities, and vocational education centers. By imposing such uncompromising control over educational content, the law effectively enables state censorship and erects significant barriers to academic freedom. Furthermore, by banning direct communication with minors on matters of sexual orientation and gender identity the law eliminates the possibility of educating adolescents about fundamental concepts of gender and sexuality even in informal settings. According to the Equality Movement’s information, although the law has not yet been enforced, consequently, no educational institutions have been fined for violating it, students have already faced rejection of academic theses on SOGIESC-related topics by their supervisors or institutional administration.’[footnote 249]

13.3.5 The International LGBTQI Youth & Student Organisation (IGLYO), ‘the world’s largest network dedicated to LGBTQI young people and their rights’[footnote 250], noted in its LGBTQI Inclusive Education Report 2025:

‘Although the Law on General Education and the Law on Higher Education formally prohibit discrimination, there are no specific policies or programmes to foster tolerance toward diverse sexual orientations and gender identities. Likewise, there are no regulatory mechanisms in place to address bullying based on SOGIESC grounds.’[footnote 251]

13.3.6 The same report noted:

‘There is currently no mandatory teacher training on LGBTQI awareness for school teachers. NGOs have typically encountered obstacles in their efforts to promote awareness-raising initiatives among teachers…

‘The LGBTQI community organisation’s attempts to collaborate with relevant state institutions to train school teachers on gender and sexuality issues have largely been rejected. The situation has been further exacerbated by the adoption of the anti-LGBTQI law, which prohibits such discussions within formal educational institutions.’[footnote 252]

13.3.7 The same report stated: ‘Despite widespread LGBTQIphobia [sic] in educational institutions in Georgia, the government has failed to establish effective mechanisms to prevent and mitigate such incidents.’[footnote 253]

13.4 Access to employment

13.4.1 The USSD 2023 Report observed: ‘LGBTQI+ activists said discrimination in the workplace based on gender identity and sexual orientation remained widespread and underreported.’[footnote 254]

13.4.2 UN Women’s Gender Equality Attitudes Study in Georgia, implemented from January to February 2024 to measure the prevalence of discriminatory attitudes and gender-based stereotypes, noted: ‘The public is mostly in agreement that being hired as skilled workers is difficult for … LGBTQI+ individuals (lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer and intersex) who are public about their sexual orientation (61 per cent).’[footnote 255]

13.4.3 The same study included the below graphic, indicating in percentages the surveyed participants’ responses to the question ‘In general, how easy is it for most sexual minority women (lesbian, bisexual, transgender, queer or intersex) who do not hide their sexual orientation / sexual minority men (gay, bisexual, transgender, queer or intersex) who do not hide their sexual orientation to be hired as skilled workers in Georgia?’ The employed 11-point scale was recoded into three categories: Scores of 0–3 were categorized as “difficult”, scores of 4–6 were categorized as “neutral”, and scores of 7–10 were categorized as “easy”[footnote 256].

13.4.4 The OFPRA 2025 Report noted:

‘Most LGBT+ persons are integrated into the labour market, primarily in the service and cultural sectors, but more than half partially or completely conceal their gender identity and/or sexual orientation at work. As is often the case in Georgia, employment is frequently precarious and poorly paid, leading many individuals to hold multiple jobs: in 2020, 68% of LGBT+ persons were employed, and among them one in five held at least two jobs. These data derive from a study conducted before the COVID-19 pandemic, during which more than two out of three LGBT+ persons lost their jobs. Nearly one LGBT+ person in three reported experiencing discrimination in the workplace, and the majority did not seek assistance, either because they considered it unnecessary or believed that nothing could be done.’[footnote 257]

13.4.5 The OFPRA 2025 Report further observed:

‘Transgender persons, particularly transgender women, face greater exclusion from the labour market, notably because of the personal identification documents they are required to present. They are also the group most exposed to prostitution, often entering sex work after experiencing violence in previous employment. A quarter were minors when they began engaging in prostitution, and nearly 90% reported having experienced violence at the hands of a client.’[footnote 258]

2. Exclusion

2.1.1 Decision makers must consider whether there are serious reasons to apply one (or more) of the exclusion clauses. Each case must be considered on its individual facts.

2.1.2 If the person is excluded from the Refugee Convention, they will also be excluded from a grant of humanitarian protection, which has a wider range of exclusions than refugee status.

2.1.3 For guidance on exclusion and restricted leave, see the Asylum Instruction on Exclusion under Articles 1F and 33(2) of the Refugee Convention, Humanitarian Protection and the instruction on Restricted Leave.

3. Convention reason(s)

3.1.1 Actual or imputed particular social group (PSG).

3.1.2 LGBT+ people form a PSG in Georgia within the meaning of the Refugee Convention because they share an innate characteristic or a common background that cannot be changed, or share a characteristic or belief that is so fundamental to identity or conscience that a person should not be forced to renounce it and have a distinct identity in Georgia because the group is perceived as being different by the surrounding society.

3.1.3 Although people of diverse SOGIE in Georgia form a PSG, establishing such membership is not sufficient to be recognised as a refugee. The question to be addressed is whether the person has a well-founded fear of persecution on account of their membership of such a group.

3.1.4 For further guidance on the 5 Refugee Convention grounds, see the Asylum Instructions on Assessing Credibility and Refugee Status.

4. Risk

4.1 Risk from the state

4.1.1 LGBT+ people in Georgia are, in general, unlikely to face a real risk of persecution or serious harm from the state. The onus is on the person to demonstrate otherwise.

4.1.2 Consensual same-sex sexual acts are not prohibited (see Provisions relating to same-sex relationships, marriage, and civil union).

4.1.3 The Constitution of Georgia stipulates that all persons are equal before the law and prohibits any form of discrimination, although it does not explicitly prohibit discrimination based on sexual orientation, gender identity or expression. Other laws contain non-discrimination provisions relating to sex or sexual orientation. In 2025, laws that had explicitly protected gender identity were amended. While protections based on sexual orientation remain in place, gender identity and gender expression were removed as protected characteristics under anti-discrimination legislation and intolerance on the ground of gender or gender identity is no longer considered an aggravating circumstance under the Criminal Code, a provision that had rarely been enforced previously (see Anti-discrimination provisions and New state policy and legislation affecting LGBT+ people).

4.1.4 The Law on the Protection of Family Values and Minors, adopted in 2024, introduced a range of restrictions affecting LGBT+ people. The law prohibits ‘popularisation’, defined as the dissemination of information that may be regarded as promoting or presenting same-sex relationships, diverse sexual orientations or gender identities in a positive light. Restrictions apply to media, educational materials, demonstrations and assemblies, as well as other forms of public communication. ‘Popularisation’ in education and advertising is punishable through fines set out in the Administrative Offences Code of Georgia. The legislation defines ‘popularisation’ broadly, leaving scope for varying interpretations as to what expressions are prohibited. Civil Society Organisations (CSOs) report self-censorship in media output on LGBT+ issues, advocacy, and public awareness campaigns on sex education to avoid potential prosecution of staff (see Provisions relating to awareness-raising and activism, Support organisations and New state policy and legislation affecting LGBT+ people).

4.1.5 The 2024 Law on the Protection of Family Values and Minors furthermore prohibits legal recognition of same-sex unions as marriage, including where people have married abroad. Its definition of marriage as a union of a woman and a man for the purpose of founding a family had previously been introduced by a 2017 amendment to the Georgian constitution (see Provisions relating to same-sex relationships, marriage, and civil union).

4.1.6 The 2024 Law on the Protection of Family Values and Minors also restricts adoption and fostering to heterosexual individuals. Prior to the adoption of the 2024 law, Georgian law did not expressly prohibit adoption by LGBT+ people and single individuals were able to adopt, subject to statutory requirements. As Georgian law did not recognise same-sex marriages or civil unions, same-sex couples did not have a legal avenue to adopt jointly as a couple (see Provisions relating to same-sex relationships, marriage, and civil union).
